title: Detection of Email Addresses
summary: This detection strategy covers the collection of email addresses, the technique where an adversary gathers valid staff addresses from public sources, guessed naming schemes, mail server responses and directory lookups so that later phishing messages actually reach a person. It matters because a mail gateway can block a bad message only after the address exists, and the collection step itself is quiet: it appears as directory enumeration against a mail service, bulk address validation probes to simple mail transfer protocol ports, and larger than usual reads of the corporate address book by one identity. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail server connection and recipient rejection logs, cloud mail audit logs for directory and address book reads, directory service query logs, and web proxy logs showing address scraping sites. Detection fails because marketing tools, recruitment platforms and mail hygiene services all validate address lists legitimately and look identical to an enumeration attempt at low volume.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for someone building a list of company email addresses. Attackers test which names are real before sending phishing mail. The rule watches for many address checks from one source. It also watches for large reads of the company address book.
beginner.whyItMatters: A phishing message needs a real address to arrive. Attackers collect addresses long before they send anything. Your mail filter only sees the message at the end. If you notice the collection early, you can block the sender and warn the staff who were listed.
howItWorks: Mail servers record every connection, every recipient address they were asked about and whether that address exists.
Directory services record queries that list users and mail attributes, called lightweight directory access protocol searches.
Those logs are collected by the security monitoring platform with the source address and the account that made the request.
The rule counts how many distinct recipient addresses one source tests in a short window.
It also flags directory searches that read the whole address book rather than one named person.
An alert lists the source, the number of addresses confirmed as valid and the accounts that ran the searches.
beginner.example: Think of a caller who phones a hotel reception. The caller asks, room by room, whether a guest with a certain name is staying there. One question is normal. Two hundred questions in ten minutes shows someone building a guest list. This detection listens for the same pattern on your mail service.
takeaways: Address collection is a mail server and directory event, not an endpoint event.
A high rate of valid recipient confirmations from one source is the strongest signal.
Address books are read in bulk by some tools, so check which accounts do that.

objectives: Explain why valid email addresses are valuable to an adversary before phishing starts.
Identify mail server and directory log fields that record address enumeration.
Write a rule that counts distinct recipient addresses tested per source address.
Describe how to distinguish a marketing validation run from hostile enumeration.
Explain how collected addresses feed later phishing for information and access.
dataSources: Mail transfer agent connection logs recording the source address, the recipient address and the accept or reject result
Cloud mail audit logs for address book reads, contact exports and directory search operations
Directory service query logs showing lightweight directory access protocol searches for mail attributes
Secure web gateway logs showing requests to people search and address scraping websites
Mail gateway logs for messages sent to a large number of invalid recipient addresses in one transaction
logic: The pattern is one source address or account testing many candidate recipient addresses in a short window, where the naming scheme is predictable and the server responses reveal which addresses exist, or a directory search that reads mail attributes for the whole organisation instead of a named person. The fields that must be correlated are the source address and its reputation, the number of distinct recipient addresses attempted, the accept or reject results, the account and client used for directory reads, and whether the source later appeared in mail gateway logs as a sender. The benign case is a mail hygiene or marketing platform validating a consented list from a documented range on a schedule; the malicious case is a burst of guesses that mirrors the corporate first name dot last name pattern from a hosting address, followed by directory reads by an account that normally never searches the directory.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Recipient Address Enumeration Against Mail Service
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: smtp
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action: 'rcpt_probe'
#     result|contains: 'reject'
#   filter_partners:
#     source_ip|cidr:
#       - '192[.]0[.]2[.]0/24'
#   condition: selection and not filter_partners | count(distinct recipient) by source_ip > 100 within 10m
# level: medium
falsePositives: Marketing automation platforms that validate a customer list before a campaign and use the company naming pattern
Migration tools that import contacts and test each address against the new mail service
Mail hygiene services that probe recipient validity during normal inbound filtering
Recruitment systems that check whether candidate addresses are deliverable before sending offers
tuningNotes: Allow list the documented source ranges of your marketing, recruitment and mail hygiene providers, and require a threshold well above their largest single campaign. Baseline directory read volume per service account for thirty days, then alert on accounts that exceed ten times their own median. Scope the rule to the externally reachable mail listener so internal application mail does not generate noise. This narrowing loses detection of slow enumeration spread over days from rotating addresses, so add a weekly rule that compares the count of rejected recipient addresses per source against the prior week and keeps any source that appears in both mail and directory telemetry.
